To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) cerebral blood flow closely followed changes in blood pressure; (2) cerebral blood flow and cortical oxygenation were inversely related; (3) MCAv pulsation increased with hypotension and decreased with hypertension; and (4) the plateau region is not a static region, but rather it changes with changes in blood pressure.

in healthy humans cerebral blood flow closely followed pharmacologically-induced changes in blood flow pressure, with a slope of 0.82 cm · s−1 · mm Hg−1; cerebral oxygenation was inversely related to blood flow pressure with a slope of −0.18%/ mm Hg− 1 and MCAv mean of −0.26%/ cm · s− 1; and there was an increase in pulsatility with progressive hypotention.

cerebral blood flow is tightly regulated in otherwise healthy humans, but with progressive hypotensive or hypertensive challenges, there are differential changes of cerebral oxygenation and middle cerebral artery mean velocity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantification of cerebral autoregulation.
the relationship between blood pressure and cerebral perfusion and oxygenation.
the quantification of cerebral autoregulation in healthy humans over an extended range of arterial pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the slope of the plateau of CA is not a reliable indicator of the status of CA.
CA is a dynamic process and that a static CA is not an appropriate term.
the static CA in otherwise healthy humans is a linear function over a wide range (40 to 125 mm Hg), with a slope of ≈0.8% change in MCAv per millimeter of change in mean blood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cerebral circulation is highly sensitive to changes in blood pressure, but that this sensitivity is not constant across the full range of blood pressures.
CA is not a fixed relationship, but is dependent upon the level of blood pressure and the degree of autoregulation.

cerebral autoregulation is not a single process but a complex interaction between the brain, cerebral vasculature, and blood pressure that is influenced by a variety of physiological and pathological factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CA is a complex process that is influenced by a variety of factors, including blood pressure.
the slope of the plateau in the relationship between cerebral blood flow and blood pressure does not imply a defective autoregulation.
the concept of a plateau in cerebral perfusion pressure is not valid.
